slides.narration: After the Second World War, the nations wanted a body that could prevent another such disaster. In this part we see how the United Nations was born, what it aims to do, and how two of its main organs, the General Assembly and the Security Council, are organised and work.

slides.narration: The Charter set up six principal organs. The General Assembly includes every member. The Security Council keeps the peace. The Economic and Social Council handles cooperation. The International Court of Justice settles legal disputes. The Secretariat is the staff, and the Trusteeship Council's work is now suspended.

slides.heading: The birth of the United Nations
slides.body_md: From **San Francisco** to **New York**.

rows: Charter comes into force: United Nations Day

visual.alt: Table of the birth of the United Nations: Charter signed at San Francisco on 26 June 1945; it came into force on 24 October 1945, now United Nations Day; 51 original members including India; 193 member states as of 2024

slides.narration: Delegates signed the Charter at San Francisco on the twenty-sixth of June nineteen forty-five. It came into force on the twenty-fourth of October that year, now celebrated as United Nations Day. There were fifty-one original members, including India. As of twenty twenty-four there were one hundred and ninety-three.

slides.heading: Quick check: the Charter
slides.body_md: In which month of 1945 was the Charter signed?
slides.narration: Think back to the slide you just saw. In which month did the delegates sign the Charter?

slides.heading: The objectives
slides.body_md: What the United Nations was set up to do (paraphrased).

rows: Prevent and stop wars; settle disputes peacefully
Respect equal rights and self-determination of peoples
Solve economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems together
Respect rights and freedoms for all, without distinction
A meeting place where nations coordinate their efforts

visual.alt: Table of the objectives of the United Nations, paraphrased: maintaining peace and security; friendly relations based on equal rights; international cooperation on economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems; promoting human rights; and being a centre for harmonising the actions of nations

slides.narration: The first aim is to maintain international peace and security. The others are to develop friendly relations among nations, to cooperate in solving economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems, to promote respect for human rights, and to be a centre where nations bring their actions into harmony.

slides.heading: Learning from the League
columns:
**The League of Nations**

- Founded **1920**
- The **USA** never joined
- No effective way to stop **aggressors**

**The United Nations**

- Founded **1945**
- All the **great powers** joined
- **Security Council** can order sanctions and force

rows: All great powers members from the start
Security Council can order sanctions and military action

visual.alt: Comparison table of the League of Nations and the United Nations: the League founded 1920 without the USA and with no effective means of enforcement, seated in Geneva; the United Nations founded 1945 with all the great powers, a Security Council able to order sanctions and military action, and its headquarters in New York

slides.narration: The founders learnt from the League's failure. The League had no effective way to stop aggressors, and the United States never joined it. The United Nations brought in all the great powers from the start and gave its Security Council the power to order sanctions and even military action.

slides.heading: The General Assembly: who sits there
slides.body_md: Every member, **one vote**.

rows: Simple majority of members present and voting
Two-thirds majority of members present and voting
Regular session every year from September; special sessions

visual.alt: Table of the General Assembly: all member states, up to five representatives each, one vote per state, simple majority on ordinary questions, two-thirds majority on important questions, a regular session every year from September and special sessions

slides.narration: Every member state sits in the General Assembly. A state may send up to five representatives, but it has only one vote, whatever its size. Ordinary questions need a simple majority. Important questions, such as admitting members or the budget, need two-thirds of the members present and voting.

slides.heading: Quick check: equal votes
slides.body_md: True or false: in the General Assembly, a very small state has the same single vote as the largest.
slides.narration: Recall how voting works in the General Assembly. Does size change the number of votes?

slides.heading: What the General Assembly does
slides.body_md: Five kinds of **functions**.

rows: Discusses any matter within the Charter and makes recommendations
Elects non-permanent Security Council members and Economic and Social Council members
Elects ICJ judges; admits members and appoints the Secretary-General on the Council's recommendation
Approves the budget and fixes contributions

visual.alt: Table of the functions of the General Assembly: deliberative, elective, joint functions with the Security Council such as electing judges, admitting members and appointing the Secretary-General, budgetary, and constituent

slides.narration: The General Assembly discusses any matter within the Charter and makes recommendations. It elects the non-permanent members of the Security Council. Together with the Council it elects the judges of the Court, admits members and appoints the Secretary-General. It approves the budget and can propose amendments to the Charter.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the two-thirds rule
slides.body_md: An imagined vote on admitting a new member.
bullets: Step 1: count members **present and voting**: 180.
Step 2: two-thirds of 180 is **120**.
Step 3: compare with a simple majority to see the difference.

visual.alt: Worked example table: with 180 members present and voting, an important question needs two-thirds, that is 120 votes, while a simple majority would be 91
visual.caption: Imagined vote.

slides.narration: Suppose one hundred and eighty members are present and voting on admitting a new state. Admission is an important question, so two-thirds are needed. Two-thirds of one hundred and eighty is one hundred and twenty. A simple majority would have been only ninety-one, so the higher rule protects big decisions.

slides.heading: The Security Council: fifteen members
slides.body_md: **Five permanent**, **ten elected**.

rows: Named in the Charter: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, the United States
Elected by the General Assembly for 2 years; five each year

visual.alt: Table of the Security Council's 15 members: five permanent members named in the Charter, China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States, with the veto; and 10 non-permanent members elected by the General Assembly for 2 years, five each year, without the veto

slides.narration: The Security Council has fifteen members. Five are permanent: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States. The other ten are elected by the General Assembly for two years, five each year, and a retiring member cannot be re-elected at once. Only the permanent members hold the veto.

slides.heading: Quick check: elected seats
slides.body_md: The Security Council has five permanent and ___ non-permanent members.
slides.narration: How many members of the Security Council are elected for two-year terms?

slides.heading: The veto
slides.body_md: A substantive decision needs **9 yes votes** and **no "no"** from a permanent member.

visual.caption: Imagined vote, drawn by SOYL.

slides.narration: On procedural matters, any nine votes are enough. On substantive matters, a decision needs nine votes and no negative vote from a permanent member. A single no from one of the five is a veto and defeats the resolution. By long practice, a permanent member that abstains does not block it.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: does it pass?
slides.body_md: Apply the rule to four imagined votes.
bullets: Step 1: count the **yes** votes: at least nine?
Step 2: did any **permanent** member vote **no**?
Step 3: an **abstention** is not a veto.

visual.alt: Worked example table of four imagined Security Council votes on substantive matters: A with 11 yes and one permanent no fails; B with 9 yes and one permanent abstention passes; C with 8 yes fails; D with 13 yes and no veto passes
visual.caption: Rule: at least 9 yes votes and no "no" from a permanent member.

slides.narration: Test four imagined votes. Vote A had eleven yes votes but one permanent member voted no, so it fails. Vote B had nine yes votes and a permanent member abstained, so it passes. Vote C had only eight yes votes, so it fails. Vote D had thirteen and no veto, so it passes.

slides.heading: Quick check: who holds the veto?
slides.body_md: Who among the following can use the veto?
slides.narration: Is the veto held by every Council member, or only by some of them?

slides.heading: How the Council keeps the peace
slides.body_md: From **investigation** to **action**.

nodes.label: Investigates a dispute that may threaten peace
Recommends peaceful settlement
Orders economic sanctions if needed
Authorises military action or sends peacekeepers
Recommends new members and the Secretary-General

visual.alt: Flow of the Security Council's functions: investigating disputes, recommending peaceful settlement, ordering economic sanctions, authorising military action or sending peacekeepers, and recommending new members and the Secretary-General
visual.caption: From talks to action.

slides.narration: The Security Council investigates any dispute that may threaten peace and recommends peaceful ways to settle it. If a threat continues, it can order economic sanctions, and if those fail, it can authorise military action or send peacekeepers. It also recommends new members and the Secretary-General to the General Assembly.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

nodes.label: Charter signed June 1945; in force 24 October 1945
Objectives: peace, friendly relations, cooperation, human rights
General Assembly: all members, one vote each
Security Council: 15 members, five with the veto
Substantive decisions: 9 votes and no veto

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: the Charter signed in June 1945 and in force on 24 October 1945; objectives of peace, friendly relations, cooperation and human rights; the General Assembly of all members with one vote each; the Security Council of 15 members, five with the veto; substantive decisions need 9 votes and no veto
visual.caption: Part 1 in five lines.

slides.narration: To sum up Part One. The Charter was signed in June nineteen forty-five and came into force on the twenty-fourth of October. The United Nations works for peace, friendly relations, cooperation and human rights. In the General Assembly every member has one vote. The Security Council has fifteen members, and five hold the veto.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: **24 October 1945**: in force; **26 June 1945**: signed.
General Assembly: **all** members, **one** vote, **two-thirds** on important questions.
Security Council: **15** members, **10** elected for **2** years.
Veto = a **no** by a permanent member on a **substantive** matter; abstention is not a veto.
Write objectives in your **own words**.

visual.alt: Worked example table of four imagined Security Council votes on substantive matters: A with 11 yes and one permanent no fails; B with 9 yes and one permanent abstention passes; C with 8 yes fails; D with 13 yes and no veto passes
visual.caption: Rule: at least 9 yes votes and no "no" from a permanent member.

slides.narration: A few tips. Do not confuse the day the Charter was signed with the day it came into force. Remember one state, one vote in the General Assembly. Learn the numbers of the Security Council, and explain the veto carefully, including the rule about abstention. Always write the objectives in your own words.

goals: State the composition, seat and functions of the International Court of Justice

slides.heading: Law, welfare and rights
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **Court**, three **agencies** and the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights**.

nodes.label: International Court of Justice
UNICEF, WHO, UNESCO
Universal Declaration of Human Rights
Organs working together

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the International Court of Justice, the agencies UNICEF, WHO and UNESCO, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and how the organs work together
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Peace is not kept by soldiers alone. In this part we meet the world's court, three agencies that work for children, health and education, and a declaration that set out the rights of every human being. Finally we see how the organs work together in a crisis.

slides.heading: The International Court of Justice
slides.body_md: The world's **court** for disputes between **states**.

rows: 15, elected for 9 years; a third every three years
General Assembly and Security Council, voting separately
No two judges of the same nationality

visual.alt: Table of the International Court of Justice: seat at the Peace Palace in The Hague; 15 judges elected for 9 years with a third elected every three years; elected by the General Assembly and the Security Council voting separately; no two judges of the same nationality

slides.narration: The International Court of Justice sits in the Peace Palace at The Hague, the only principal organ outside New York. It has fifteen judges, elected for nine years by the General Assembly and the Security Council voting separately. A third are elected every three years, and no two may share a nationality.

slides.heading: Quick check: the judges
slides.body_md: True or false: the International Court of Justice has fifteen judges.
slides.narration: Recall the number of judges on the world court.

slides.heading: What the Court does
slides.body_md: **Contentious** cases and **advisory** opinions.

nodes.label: States accept the Court's jurisdiction
Contentious case heard under international law
Majority judgment, binding and final
If not obeyed: the other party may go to the Security Council

visual.alt: Flow of a contentious case at the International Court of Justice: states accept its jurisdiction, the case is heard under international law, the majority judgment is binding and final, and if it is not obeyed the other party may go to the Security Council
visual.caption: Advisory opinions are given separately to UN organs.

slides.narration: When states accept its jurisdiction, the Court hears their legal dispute and decides it under international law. Its majority judgment is binding and final. If a party does not obey, the other may turn to the Security Council. The Court also gives advisory opinions to the General Assembly, the Council and authorised agencies.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which jurisdiction?
slides.body_md: Sort three imagined requests.
bullets: Step 1: is it a **dispute between states**? Then **contentious**.
Step 2: is a **UN organ** asking a legal question? Then **advisory**.
Step 3: is a **private person** suing? The ICJ cannot hear it.

rows: Two states dispute a shared bay
The General Assembly asks a legal question
A citizen sues a foreign government
Not possible: only states are parties

visual.alt: Worked example table: two states disputing a bay fall under contentious jurisdiction; a legal question from the General Assembly is advisory; a citizen cannot sue a foreign government because only states are parties
visual.caption: Sort the request first.

slides.narration: Practise sorting. Two states disputing a shared bay, both accepting the Court, make a contentious case. When the General Assembly asks a legal question, the Court gives an advisory opinion. A private citizen cannot sue a foreign government at the Court, because only states can be parties.

slides.heading: Three United Nations agencies
slides.body_md: **UNICEF**, **WHO** and **UNESCO**.

rows: Children's health, nutrition, clean water, emergency relief, education
Health standards, control of epidemics, immunisation, health systems
UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation)
Education and literacy, science, culture and world heritage

visual.alt: Table of three United Nations agencies: UNICEF, the United Nations Children's Fund, set up in 1946, headquarters New York, children's health, nutrition, water, relief and education; WHO, the World Health Organisation, 1948, Geneva, health standards, epidemic control, immunisation and health systems; UNESCO, 1945, Paris, education, science, culture and heritage
visual.caption: Only headquarters and functions are required.

slides.narration: Specialised agencies carry the work of the United Nations into daily life. The United Nations Children's Fund, in New York, works for children's health, food, water and schooling. The World Health Organisation, in Geneva, guards world health. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation, in Paris, works for learning, science and culture.

slides.heading: Quick check: which city?
slides.body_md: Which agency in this list has its headquarters in Geneva?
slides.narration: Match the agency with its home city. Which one is based in Geneva?

slides.heading: Agencies at work
slides.body_md: What each agency **does**.
bullets: **UNICEF:** immunisation, nutrition, clean water, emergency relief, education for children.
**WHO:** international health standards, control of epidemics, help to health systems.
**UNESCO:** literacy and education, science, culture, the World Heritage List.

rows: Children's health, nutrition, clean water, emergency relief, education
Health standards, control of epidemics, immunisation, health systems
UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation)
Education and literacy, science, culture and world heritage

visual.alt: Table of three United Nations agencies: UNICEF, the United Nations Children's Fund, set up in 1946, headquarters New York, children's health, nutrition, water, relief and education; WHO, the World Health Organisation, 1948, Geneva, health standards, epidemic control, immunisation and health systems; UNESCO, 1945, Paris, education, science, culture and heritage
visual.caption: Only headquarters and functions are required.

slides.narration: Think of the agencies by what they do. The Children's Fund vaccinates infants, feeds children and helps them in emergencies. The World Health Organisation sets health standards and leads the fight against epidemics. The educational and cultural organisation spreads literacy, links scientists and protects heritage sites on its world list.

slides.heading: Quick check: Paris
slides.body_md: UNESCO has its headquarters in the city of ___.
slides.narration: Which city is home to the agency for education, science and culture?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: choosing the agency
slides.body_md: Match each **imagined need** to an agency, with a reason.
bullets: Step 1: decide the **field**: health, children, or education and culture.
Step 2: name the **agency**.
Step 3: give the **reason** in one line.

visual.alt: Worked example table matching needs to agencies: a fever outbreak to the WHO, which controls epidemics; flood-hit children to UNICEF, which gives emergency relief; restoring a temple complex to UNESCO, which protects heritage
visual.caption: Name the agency, then give the reason.

slides.narration: Match needs to agencies. A district fighting a fever outbreak needs the World Health Organisation, which controls epidemics. Flood-hit children without food need the Children's Fund. A town restoring an old temple complex needs the organisation for education, science and culture, which protects heritage. Always add a reason.

slides.heading: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
slides.body_md: A **common standard** of rights for everyone.

nodes.label: 10 December 1948: adopted by the General Assembly in Paris
Sets out basic rights and freedoms for every person
A common standard, not a binding treaty
Inspired constitutions and later treaties on rights

visual.alt: Flow about the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: adopted by the General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948; it sets out basic rights and freedoms for every person; it is a common standard rather than a binding treaty; it inspired constitutions and later treaties
visual.caption: Meaning only, as the syllabus requires.

slides.narration: On the tenth of December nineteen forty-eight, the General Assembly, meeting in Paris, adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It sets out the basic rights and freedoms that every person should enjoy. It is not a binding treaty, but it has inspired many constitutions and later agreements. The day is now Human Rights Day.

slides.heading: Quick check: the year
slides.body_md: In which year did the General Assembly adopt the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
slides.narration: Was the Declaration adopted in the same year as the Charter, or later?

slides.heading: Why the Declaration still matters
columns:
**What it is not**

- Not a **treaty** that courts enforce
- Not a law of the **Security Council**
- Not limited to **some** countries

**What it has done**

- Set a **common standard** for all
- **Inspired** constitutions, including fundamental rights
- Led to later **treaties** on rights

nodes.label: 10 December 1948: adopted by the General Assembly in Paris
Sets out basic rights and freedoms for every person
A common standard, not a binding treaty
Inspired constitutions and later treaties on rights

visual.alt: Flow about the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: adopted by the General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948; it sets out basic rights and freedoms for every person; it is a common standard rather than a binding treaty; it inspired constitutions and later treaties
visual.caption: Meaning only, as the syllabus requires.

slides.narration: The Declaration is not a treaty that any court enforces, and it is not a law of the Security Council. Yet it matters a great deal. It gave the world one common standard of rights, it inspired many constitutions, including chapters on fundamental rights, and later treaties on rights were built upon it.

slides.heading: Organs working together
slides.body_md: An **imagined** crisis: one state invades another.

nodes.label: Security Council: ceasefire, sanctions, peacekeepers
If blocked by a veto: General Assembly discusses and recommends

sections.heading: 1. Birth and objectives
sections.body_md:
- **Charter** signed at **San Francisco** on **26 June 1945**; in force on **24 October 1945** (United Nations Day). Headquarters: **New York**.
- **51 original members**, including **India**; **193** members as of 2024.
- **Objectives (paraphrased):** maintain international **peace and security**; develop **friendly relations** based on equal rights and self-determination; achieve **international cooperation** on economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems; promote **human rights**; be a **centre** for harmonising the actions of nations.
- Learning from the **League**: all great powers joined, and the Security Council can **enforce** decisions.

key_terms.definition_md: The founding treaty of the United Nations, setting out its aims, organs and rules.
The principle that every member state, large or small, has equal standing.

sections.heading: 2. The General Assembly
sections.body_md:
- **Composition:** all member states; up to **five representatives**, **one vote** each.
- **Voting:** simple majority on ordinary questions; **two-thirds** of members present and voting on **important** questions (peace and security, admission, budget).
- **Sessions:** a regular session every year from **September**; special sessions when needed.
- **Functions:** deliberative (discusses any matter, recommends); elective (non-permanent Security Council members, Economic and Social Council); with the Security Council, elects **ICJ judges**, **admits members** and **appoints the Secretary-General**; **budgetary**; **constituent** (amendments).

sections.heading: 3. The Security Council and the veto
sections.body_md:
- **15 members:** **five permanent** (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, the United States) and **10 non-permanent**, elected for **2 years**, five each year, not immediately re-eligible.
- **Voting:** procedural matters, any **nine** votes; substantive matters, **nine** votes including the **concurring votes** of the permanent members. A **no** by a permanent member is a **veto**; by practice an **abstention** is not.
- **Functions:** investigate disputes, recommend settlement, order **sanctions**, authorise **military action** and **peacekeeping**, recommend members and the Secretary-General.
- **Debate:** the veto keeps the great powers inside the UN but can **paralyse** the Council; reforms have been discussed.

key_terms.definition_md: The power of a permanent member to block a substantive decision by voting against it.
Economic or other penalties ordered against a state that threatens peace.

sections.heading: 4. The International Court of Justice
sections.body_md:
- **Seat:** Peace Palace, **The Hague**.
- **15 judges**, elected by the **General Assembly and the Security Council** voting separately, for **9 years**; a third every three years; **no two of the same nationality**.
- **Contentious jurisdiction:** legal disputes between **states** that accept it; judgments are **binding and final**; if not obeyed, the other party may approach the Security Council.
- **Advisory jurisdiction:** opinions on legal questions for the General Assembly, the Security Council and authorised agencies.
- Individuals **cannot** bring cases.

key_terms.definition_md: The Court's power to decide legal disputes between states.
The Court's legal opinion given at the request of a UN organ or agency.

sections.heading: 5. UNICEF, WHO and UNESCO
sections.body_md:
- **UNICEF** (United Nations Children's Fund), set up **1946**, **New York**: child health and immunisation, nutrition, clean water, emergency relief, education.
- **WHO** (World Health Organisation), **1948**, **Geneva**: international health standards, control of epidemics, immunisation campaigns, help to health systems. World Health Day: **7 April**.
- **UNESCO** (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation), **1945**, **Paris**: education and literacy, science, culture, the **World Heritage List**.
- Only **headquarters and functions** are required.

sections.heading: 6. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
sections.body_md:
- Adopted by the **General Assembly** in **Paris** on **10 December 1948** (Human Rights Day).
- **Meaning:** a statement of the basic **rights and freedoms** every person should enjoy, without distinction, as a **common standard** for all peoples and nations.
- **Not a binding treaty**, but it has **inspired** national constitutions (including fundamental rights) and later treaties on rights.
- Only its **meaning** is required; explain it in your own words.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing **26 June** as the founding day (that was the signing; the UN came into existence on **24 October 1945**).
- Giving the General Assembly the veto (it has **none**).
- Saying any **no** vote is a veto (only a **permanent** member's no on a **substantive** matter).
- Treating an **abstention** as a veto.
- Saying individuals can sue at the **ICJ** (only **states**).
- Mixing up the cities: UNICEF **New York**, WHO **Geneva**, UNESCO **Paris**, ICJ **The Hague**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one point per mark; the 4-mark part often asks you to explain, apply or evaluate.

questions.stem_md: Every year 24 October is observed as United Nations Day. What happened on that date in 1945?

options.text_md: The Charter was first signed at San Francisco
The United Nations formally came into existence after enough states ratified its Charter
The League of Nations held its first meeting
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The United Nations formally came into existence after enough states ratified its Charter. The Charter was signed on 26 June 1945 and came into force on 24 October 1945, now United Nations Day. The League first met in 1920, and the Declaration was adopted in 1948.

questions.stem_md: A Class 10 class in Kochi is writing to the main headquarters of the United Nations. In which city should the letter be addressed?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** New York. The headquarters of the United Nations is in New York. Geneva hosts several UN offices and the WHO, The Hague the ICJ, and Paris UNESCO.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is the first and chief objective of the United Nations named in its Charter?

options.text_md: To maintain international peace and security
To create a single world government
To manage the trade of member states
To choose the governments of new nations

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** To maintain international peace and security. Maintaining international peace and security comes first among the aims. The UN is not a world government and does not run members' trade or choose their governments.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined neighbouring countries, Avalor and Brenn, agree to accept UN help to share a river fairly and to run joint schools for refugee children. Which objectives of the United Nations does this serve?

options.text_md: Only the collection of member contributions
Making Avalor a permanent member of the Security Council
Friendly relations among nations and international cooperation on social problems
Ending the sovereign equality of member states

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Friendly relations among nations and international cooperation on social problems. Settling a shared problem and cooperating on education serve the aims of friendly relations and cooperation on economic, social and humanitarian problems. The other options are not UN objectives.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The founders of the United Nations gave its Security Council the power to order sanctions and military action.

**Reason (R):** The League of Nations had failed partly because it had no effective means to stop aggressors.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: learning from the League's failure over Manchuria and Abyssinia, the founders gave the Security Council powers to enforce its decisions.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The United Nations is a world government that can overrule the laws of its member states.

**Reason (R):** The Charter is based on the sovereign equality of all its members.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: the UN is an organisation of sovereign states, not a world government. R is true: the Charter rests on the sovereign equality of members.

questions.stem_md: Apart from keeping peace, state two other objectives set out for the United Nations in 1945.
questions.solution_md: Any two objectives other than peace.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. To develop **friendly relations** among nations based on **equal rights** and self-determination of peoples.
2. To achieve **international cooperation** in solving **economic, social, cultural and humanitarian** problems and to promote **human rights**.

questions.stem_md: Give two ways in which the United Nations was designed to be stronger than the League of Nations it replaced.
questions.solution_md: Enforcement powers; membership of the great powers.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Its **Security Council** can order **sanctions** and **military action**, which the League could not enforce.
2. The great powers, including the **USA**, joined from the start, and the five permanent members were given a **special role**.

questions.stem_md: Which organ of the United Nations includes every member state, each with one vote?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The General Assembly. Every member sits in the General Assembly with one vote. The Security Council has 15 members, the Court 15 judges, and the Secretariat is the staff.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined General Assembly vote on admitting a new member, 180 members are present and voting. What is the least number of yes votes needed?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 120. Admission is an important question, needing a two-thirds majority of members present and voting: two-thirds of 180 is 120. 91 would be a simple majority; 97 and 129 follow no rule.

questions.stem_md: Which organ approves the budget of the United Nations and decides how much each member contributes?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The General Assembly. The General Assembly has the budgetary function: it approves the budget and apportions contributions among members.

questions.stem_md: Each year the General Assembly fills five seats on another organ for two-year terms. Which seats are these?

options.text_md: Permanent seats on the Security Council
Non-permanent seats on the Security Council
Judgeships of the International Court of Justice by itself alone
Headships of UNICEF, WHO and UNESCO

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Non-permanent seats on the Security Council. The Assembly elects the 10 non-permanent Council members for 2-year terms, five each year. Permanent seats are fixed by the Charter, and ICJ judges are elected by the Assembly and the Council together.

questions.stem_md: How is the Secretary-General of the United Nations appointed?

options.text_md: By the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council
By the International Court of Justice
By a direct vote of the people of member states

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** By the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council. The General Assembly appoints the Secretary-General on the Security Council's recommendation, so both organs take part.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A resolution passed by the General Assembly on a world problem is binding on every member state.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. General Assembly resolutions are mostly recommendations that carry moral and political weight; the Security Council's decisions on peace and security are the ones members are bound to carry out.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The General Assembly is often described as a world forum or parliament of nations.

**Reason (R):** Every member state, large or small, is represented in it with an equal vote and may raise any matter within the Charter.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: universal membership, equal votes and the freedom to discuss any matter make the Assembly a forum where every nation is heard.

questions.stem_md: Describe how the General Assembly is made up and how it takes a decision on an important question.
questions.solution_md: Composition and the two-thirds rule.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **All member states** are members; each may send up to **five representatives** but has **one vote**.
2. Decisions on **important questions**, such as admitting members or the budget, need a **two-thirds majority** of members present and voting.

questions.stem_md: Explain the deliberative, budgetary and constituent functions of the General Assembly, one point each.
questions.solution_md: One point for each function.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Deliberative:** it discusses any question within the scope of the Charter, such as peace, development or human rights, and makes **recommendations**.
2. **Budgetary:** it **approves the budget** and fixes each member's **contribution**.
3. **Constituent:** it can propose **amendments to the Charter**, which take effect when ratified by two-thirds of members, including all permanent members of the Security Council.

questions.stem_md:
With reference to the General Assembly, answer the following.

(i) Describe its composition and voting. **[3]**
(ii) Explain its electoral functions. **[3]**
(iii) Why is it said that small nations have a real voice in the General Assembly? Give four reasons. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Composition and voting; elections; voice of small nations.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Every member state** belongs to the General Assembly. Each may send up to **five representatives**, but each state has **one vote**. Ordinary questions are decided by a **simple majority**; **important questions** need a **two-thirds majority** of members present and voting.

(ii) It elects the **ten non-permanent** members of the Security Council and the members of the **Economic and Social Council**. With the Security Council it elects the **judges** of the International Court of Justice, and on the Council's recommendation it **admits new members** and **appoints the Secretary-General**.

(iii) 1. Every state has an **equal vote**, whatever its size or power.
2. There is **no veto** in the Assembly.
3. Small states together form a **majority** and can pass resolutions.
4. Any member may **raise any issue** within the Charter, so its concerns reach the whole world.

questions.stem_md: How many members make up the Security Council at present?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 15. The Council has 15 members: five permanent and ten non-permanent. It had 11 members until it was enlarged in 1965; 193 is the whole membership of the UN.

questions.stem_md: Which group lists exactly the five permanent members of the Security Council?

options.text_md: China, India, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States
France, Germany, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States
China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States
Brazil, China, France, Russia and the United States

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States. The five permanent members are China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States. India, Japan, Germany and Brazil are not permanent members.

questions.stem_md: For how long does a non-permanent member serve on the Security Council?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Two years. Non-permanent members are elected by the General Assembly for 2-year terms; five seats fall vacant each year. Nine years is an ICJ judge's term.

questions.stem_md: What does the veto power of a permanent member of the Security Council allow it to do?

options.text_md: Expel any member from the UN on its own
Overrule a judgment of the International Court of Justice
Pass a resolution without any other votes
Block a decision on a substantive matter by voting against it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Block a decision on a substantive matter by voting against it. A negative vote by any permanent member defeats a substantive decision, even if nine or more members vote for it. The veto does not let a member expel others, overrule the Court or pass resolutions alone.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined Security Council vote on sending peacekeepers, 11 members vote yes and one permanent member votes no. What happens?

options.text_md: The resolution passes because more than nine members voted yes
The matter goes automatically to the International Court of Justice
The resolution fails because a permanent member has voted against it
The General Assembly must decide within one day

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The resolution fails because a permanent member has voted against it. Even with 11 yes votes, a "no" from a permanent member is a veto on a substantive matter, so the resolution fails.

questions.stem_md: In another imagined vote on sanctions, 9 members vote yes, none votes no, and one permanent member abstains. What happens?

options.text_md: The resolution fails, because every permanent member must vote yes
The resolution passes, because by practice an abstention is not treated as a veto
The resolution fails, because ten votes are needed
The vote must be repeated after one month

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The resolution passes, because by practice an abstention is not treated as a veto. By long practice an abstaining permanent member does not block a decision. With 9 yes votes and no veto, the resolution passes.

questions.stem_md: An imagined resolution on a ceasefire gets 8 yes votes, including all five permanent members, and the rest abstain. What is the result?

options.text_md: It fails, because at least nine yes votes are needed
It passes, because all permanent members agreed
It passes, because no member voted no
It fails, because abstentions count as vetoes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It fails, because at least nine yes votes are needed. A substantive decision needs at least 9 affirmative votes; 8 is not enough, even with all permanent members in favour.

questions.stem_md: An imagined state, Kordia, invades its neighbour and ignores calls to withdraw. Which UN organ can decide on binding economic sanctions against Kordia?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Security Council. Only the Security Council can take decisions on sanctions and military action that members must carry out. The Assembly can recommend, UNESCO works in education and culture, and the Court decides legal disputes.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Every member of the Security Council must keep a representative at UN headquarters at all times.

**Reason (R):** The Council must be able to meet at short notice whenever peace is threatened.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: because a crisis can arise at any moment, the Council is organised to function continuously.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A substantive resolution can pass the Security Council even if one permanent member abstains.

**Reason (R):** Every permanent member must vote yes for any decision of the Council to pass.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true: by practice an abstention is not a veto. R is false: what blocks a decision is a negative vote by a permanent member, not the lack of a yes vote.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A non-permanent member of the Security Council may be re-elected straight away for the next two-year term.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. A retiring non-permanent member is not eligible for immediate re-election.

questions.stem_md: Explain the term veto and state one criticism made of it.
questions.solution_md: Meaning; one criticism.

answer.model_answer_md: **Veto** is the power of each **permanent member** to **block** a substantive decision by voting against it, even if nine members support it. **Criticism:** it lets one great power **stop action** on a crisis, which can leave the Council **paralysed**.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the permanent and non-permanent members of the Security Council.
questions.solution_md: Permanent: five, permanent seats, veto. Non-permanent: ten, elected for two years, no veto.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **five permanent members** (China, France, Russia, the UK and the USA) hold their seats **permanently** and each has the **veto**.
2. The **ten non-permanent members** are **elected** by the General Assembly for **two years** and have **no veto**.

questions.stem_md: Mention two steps the Security Council can take when it finds a threat to international peace.
questions.solution_md: Any two steps.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It can call on the parties to settle the dispute **peacefully** and recommend terms or send a **peacekeeping** force with their consent.
2. It can order **economic sanctions** or, if they fail, **military action** by member states.

questions.solution_md: Decision plus the rule.

questions.stem_md:
With reference to the Security Council, answer the following.

(i) Describe its composition. **[3]**
(ii) How are decisions taken on procedural and on substantive matters? **[3]**
(iii) Explain four functions of the Security Council in maintaining peace. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Composition; voting; four functions.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Council has **15 members**. The **permanent** seats, held by **China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States**, number **five**. **Ten** are **non-permanent**, elected by the General Assembly for **two years**, five each year, and not eligible for immediate re-election.

(ii) Each member has **one vote**. **Procedural** matters need **nine** votes of any members. **Substantive** matters need **nine** votes including the **concurring votes** of the permanent members, so a **no** by any one of them is a **veto**; by practice an **abstention** does not block a decision.

(iii) 1. It **investigates** any dispute that may threaten peace.
2. It **recommends** peaceful methods of settlement.
3. It can order **economic sanctions** and, if needed, **military action**.
4. It sends **peacekeeping** missions and recommends the **admission** of members and the **Secretary-General**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the veto in the Security Council.

(i) Which members hold the veto, and when can it be used? **[3]**
(ii) Give three arguments made in favour of the veto. **[3]**
(iii) Give four arguments made against the veto, and suggest one reform that has been discussed. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Holders and use; arguments for; arguments against and a reform.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **five permanent members**, China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States, hold the veto. It applies to **substantive** (non-procedural) decisions: a **negative vote** by any one of them defeats a resolution even if nine or more members support it.

(ii) 1. It keeps the **great powers** inside the UN, which the League had failed to do.
2. It prevents the Council from taking **military action** against a great power, which could start a **world war**.
3. Decisions backed by all the great powers are more likely to be **carried out**.

(iii) 1. It is **undemocratic**: one state can block the will of the rest.
2. It has **paralysed** the Council in many crises.
3. Permanent members may use it to protect **themselves or their allies**.
4. The five reflect the world of **1945**, not of today. **Reform discussed:** adding new permanent members or **limiting** the veto in cases of mass atrocities.

questions.stem_md: The principal judicial organ of the United Nations sits in the Peace Palace in which city?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Hague. The International Court of Justice sits at The Hague in the Netherlands; it is the only principal organ not based in New York.

questions.stem_md: Two candidates from the same imagined country, Merovia, are both popular in an ICJ election. What does the Court's rule say?

options.text_md: No two judges of the Court may be nationals of the same state, so only one can sit
Both may be elected if they win a majority
Merovia must choose one by a national vote
Both may sit but only one may vote

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** No two judges of the Court may be nationals of the same state, so only one can sit. The Court may not have two judges of the same nationality at the same time, so at most one candidate from Merovia can be a judge.

questions.stem_md: Which bodies elect the judges of the International Court of Justice?

options.text_md: The General Assembly and the Security Council, voting separately
The governments of the five permanent members

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The General Assembly and the Security Council, voting separately. A candidate must win an absolute majority in both the General Assembly and the Security Council, voting independently.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined states, Ostra and Valen, both accept the Court's jurisdiction in a dispute over fishing rights in a shared bay. Which kind of jurisdiction will the ICJ use?

options.text_md: Advisory jurisdiction, giving an opinion to the General Assembly
Contentious jurisdiction, deciding a legal dispute between states
Appellate jurisdiction over a national court

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Contentious jurisdiction, deciding a legal dispute between states. A legal dispute between states that accept the Court's jurisdiction falls under its contentious jurisdiction. The ICJ does not try individuals or hear appeals from national courts.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The International Court of Justice can give advisory opinions on legal questions.

**Reason (R):** The judges of the International Court of Justice are elected for nine years.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. Advisory opinions are given because the Charter lets the General Assembly, the Security Council and authorised agencies ask for them; the length of judges' terms is unrelated.

questions.stem_md: True or false? An imagined trader from Merovia, unhappy with a foreign government's customs seizure, can file a case against that government directly in the International Court of Justice.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Only states can be parties in contentious cases before the ICJ; individuals cannot bring cases there.

questions.stem_md: State the number of judges of the ICJ, their term, and how many are elected at a time.
questions.solution_md: Fifteen; nine years; a third every three years.

answer.model_answer_md: The Court has **15 judges**, elected for **9 years** and eligible for re-election. To keep continuity, **one-third** (five judges) is elected **every three years**.

questions.stem_md: Explain the two main functions of the International Court of Justice.
questions.solution_md: Contentious and advisory.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Contentious jurisdiction:** it decides **legal disputes between states** that accept its jurisdiction, and its judgment is **binding** on them.
2. **Advisory jurisdiction:** it gives **advisory opinions** on legal questions referred by the **General Assembly**, the **Security Council** or authorised agencies.

questions.stem_md: What qualities and rules help keep the judges of the ICJ independent and representative of the world? Give three points.
questions.solution_md: Three points on independence and representation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Judges must be persons of **high moral character** qualified for the **highest judicial offices** or recognised experts in **international law**.
2. **No two** judges may be of the **same nationality**, and the Court as a whole should represent the world's **main legal systems**.
3. They serve fixed **nine-year terms** and cannot hold any **political or administrative** office while on the Court.

questions.stem_md:
With reference to the International Court of Justice, answer the following.

(i) State where it sits and how its judges are chosen. **[3]**
(ii) What happens when two states bring a dispute before it? **[3]**
(iii) Explain four ways in which the Court helps the United Nations maintain peace. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Seat and election; procedure; contribution to peace.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Court sits in the **Peace Palace** at **The Hague**. Its **15 judges** are elected by an **absolute majority** in **both** the General Assembly and the Security Council, voting separately, for **nine-year** terms; no two may be of the **same nationality**.

(ii) Under its **contentious jurisdiction**, the states that **accept** its jurisdiction present their case. The Court applies **international law**, decides by a **majority** of judges, and its judgment is **final** and **binding** on the parties.

(iii) 1. It offers a **peaceful, legal** way to settle disputes instead of war.
2. Its **advisory opinions** guide UN organs on legal questions.
3. Its rulings help develop and clarify **international law**.
4. If a party does not obey a judgment, the other may turn to the **Security Council** for action.

questions.stem_md: Where are the headquarters of the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF)?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** New York. UNICEF has its headquarters in New York. The WHO is in Geneva and UNESCO in Paris.

questions.stem_md: An imagined state government wants an old stepwell and its carvings to be recognised on the world list of heritage sites. Which agency keeps that list?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** UNESCO. UNESCO maintains the World Heritage List and works to protect cultural and natural sites.

questions.stem_md: A village health worker runs a drive to vaccinate infants and supply clean water and nutrition packets to mothers. Which two agencies most directly support such work?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** UNICEF and the WHO. UNICEF works for children's health, nutrition and clean water, and the WHO for immunisation and disease control. UNESCO, the ICJ and the Security Council have other roles.

questions.stem_md: An imagined programme trains teachers, sets up libraries in remote towns and supports science exchanges between universities. Its work falls most clearly under which agency?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** UNESCO. Education, science and culture are UNESCO's fields. The WHO deals with health, UNICEF with children, and the General Assembly is a principal organ, not an agency.

questions.stem_md: Match each UN agency or organ with the city where it has its headquarters or seat.
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). UNICEF: New York; WHO: Geneva; UNESCO: Paris; ICJ: The Hague.

questions.stem_md: World Health Day is marked on 7 April, the date in 1948 on which the constitution of the ___ came into force.
questions.solution_md: The constitution of the World Health Organisation came into force on 7 April 1948, now World Health Day.

questions.stem_md: Name the headquarters of UNICEF and give two of its functions.
questions.solution_md: Headquarters plus two functions.

answer.model_answer_md: UNICEF is headquartered in **New York**. It works for **child health** through immunisation, nutrition and clean **water**, and gives **emergency relief** and support for **education** to children in need.

questions.stem_md: Name the headquarters of the WHO and state two of its functions.
questions.solution_md: Headquarters plus two functions.

answer.model_answer_md: The WHO is headquartered in **Geneva**. It sets **international health standards** and leads the **control of epidemic diseases**, for example through **immunisation** campaigns and help to national **health systems**.

questions.stem_md: Name the headquarters of UNESCO and give two of its functions.
questions.solution_md: Headquarters plus two functions.

answer.model_answer_md: UNESCO is headquartered in **Paris**. It promotes **education** and **literacy**, encourages **scientific** cooperation, and protects **culture** and **heritage**, for example through the World Heritage List.

questions.stem_md: For each imagined request, name the agency best suited to help and give a reason: (a) a district fighting an outbreak of a fever; (b) a flood-hit town where children lack food; (c) a town restoring an old temple complex.
questions.solution_md: One agency and reason for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **WHO**, because it leads the **control of epidemic diseases** and supports health systems.
(b) **UNICEF**, because it gives **emergency relief**, **nutrition** and clean water to **children**.
(c) **UNESCO**, because it protects **cultural heritage** and keeps the World Heritage List.

questions.stem_md:
With reference to the specialised work of the United Nations, answer the following.

(i) State the headquarters and three functions of UNICEF. **[3]**
(ii) State the headquarters and three functions of the WHO. **[3]**
(iii) State the headquarters of UNESCO and explain three of its functions; then say how its work helps peace. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Headquarters and functions of each agency.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) UNICEF, set up in **1946**, has its headquarters in **New York**. It works for **child health** through immunisation and **nutrition** for infants and mothers; it supplies **clean water** and sanitation in poor areas; and it gives **emergency relief** and support for **education** to children caught in wars and disasters.

(ii) The WHO, whose constitution came into force in **1948**, has its headquarters in **Geneva**. It sets **international health standards** for medicines and food; it leads the **control of epidemics** and organises immunisation drives; and it helps countries build **health systems**, train health workers and carry out **research**.

(iii) UNESCO has its headquarters in **Paris**. It promotes **education and literacy**, especially for adults and girls; it encourages **scientific** cooperation between countries; and it protects **culture and heritage**, including sites on the World Heritage List. It helps **peace** because it builds **understanding** among peoples through education, shared knowledge and the exchange of ideas.

questions.stem_md: Which description best fits the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?

options.text_md: A treaty that lets the ICJ punish any government that breaks it
A common standard of basic rights and freedoms that every person should enjoy, adopted by the General Assembly
A list of rights that apply only to citizens of permanent members
A law passed by the Security Council for wartime only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A common standard of basic rights and freedoms that every person should enjoy, adopted by the General Assembly. The Declaration sets out basic rights and freedoms as a common standard for all peoples and nations. It is a declaration of the General Assembly, not an enforceable treaty or a Security Council law.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Universal Declaration of Human Rights has influenced the constitutions and laws of many countries.

**Reason (R):** The Declaration was adopted by the General Assembly in Paris in 1948.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. Its influence comes from the respect it commands as a common standard of rights, not from the place or year of its adoption.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and why is it called universal?
questions.solution_md: Meaning and why universal.

answer.model_answer_md: It is a statement adopted by the **General Assembly** on **10 December 1948** listing the basic **rights and freedoms** every person should enjoy. It is called **universal** because it applies to **all people everywhere**, without distinction of race, sex, religion or nation.

questions.stem_md: Give three examples of rights included in the spirit of the Universal Declaration, and link each to a situation in an imagined school or town.
questions.solution_md: Three rights with situations.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Right to education:** a town opens a free school so that no child is turned away.
2. **Freedom of expression:** students may publish their views in the school magazine.
3. **Equality before the law:** a court hears a worker's complaint in the same way as a rich trader's.

questions.stem_md:
With reference to human rights and the United Nations, answer the following.

(i) When and by which organ was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted? What does it set out? **[3]**
(ii) How is the promotion of human rights linked to the objectives of the United Nations? **[3]**
(iii) The Declaration is not a binding treaty. Evaluate its importance in four points. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Adoption and content; link to objectives; evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) It was adopted by the **General Assembly** on **10 December 1948** in **Paris**. It sets out the basic **civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights** and freedoms that every person should enjoy, as a **common standard** for all peoples and nations.

(ii) Promoting **respect for human rights** without distinction is one of the **objectives** of the Charter. The founders believed that the denial of rights before and during the war had helped cause **conflict**, so protecting rights supports **peace** and **friendly relations**.

(iii) 1. It gave the world its first **common list** of rights.
2. It has **inspired** many national **constitutions** and laws, including chapters of fundamental rights.
3. Later **treaties** on civil, political, economic and social rights built on it.
4. It gives people and groups a **moral standard** for judging governments, though enforcement depends on states.

questions.stem_md: Put these milestones of the United Nations system in the order in which they happened.

options.text_md: UNICEF is set up as an emergency fund for children
The Charter is signed at San Francisco
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is adopted
The World Health Organisation's constitution comes into force

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (e) → (a) → (d) → (c). June 1945, October 1945, December 1946, April 1948, December 1948.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The International Court of Justice. A legal ruling on a treaty dispute between states is a matter for the International Court of Justice. The Assembly and the Council are political organs, and UNICEF works for children.

questions.stem_md: Which body in this list is NOT one of the six principal organs of the United Nations?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** UNESCO. UNESCO is a specialised agency. The six principal organs are the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council, the Trusteeship Council, the International Court of Justice and the Secretariat.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **General Assembly** includes **every member**; the **Security Council** has **15**. The Assembly mostly **recommends**, while the Council takes **decisions** on peace and security that members must carry out, and its permanent members have a **veto**.

(ii) The **International Court of Justice** sits at **The Hague**. It decides **legal disputes between states** that accept its jurisdiction and gives **advisory opinions** to UN organs.

(iii) 1. The **Security Council** meets at once, calls for a **ceasefire** and may order **sanctions** or a **peacekeeping** force.
2. If the Council is blocked by a **veto**, the **General Assembly** may discuss the crisis and **recommend** action.
3. The **International Court of Justice** may decide the **legal dispute** over the border if both states accept its jurisdiction.
4. The **Secretariat** organises the missions and reports to the organs.

questions.stem_md: An imagined newly independent island state, Lumara, applies to join the United Nations. Which route must its application follow?

options.text_md: The General Assembly alone admits it by a simple majority
The International Court of Justice examines and admits it
The Secretary-General admits it after a visit
The Security Council recommends admission, then the General Assembly decides by a two-thirds majority

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Security Council recommends admission, then the General Assembly decides by a two-thirds majority. Admission needs a recommendation of the Security Council (where a permanent member's veto applies) followed by a two-thirds vote of the General Assembly.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined case, the ICJ rules for Ostra in a fishing dispute, but Valen refuses to obey the judgment. What can Ostra do under the Charter?

options.text_md: Appeal to a higher world court
Ask UNESCO to enforce the judgment
Turn to the Security Council, which may decide on measures to give effect to the judgment
Nothing, since ICJ judgments are only advice

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Turn to the Security Council, which may decide on measures to give effect to the judgment. ICJ judgments in contentious cases are binding and final, with no appeal; if a party does not comply, the other may go to the Security Council. UNESCO has no such role.

questions.stem_md: A small imagined coastal state, not on the Security Council, wants to raise the danger of rising seas before every nation and win wide support for a resolution. Which organ best suits this aim, and why?

options.text_md: The Security Council, because it is the largest organ
The General Assembly, because all members sit there with equal votes and any matter within the Charter can be discussed
The International Court of Justice, because it makes laws for states
UNICEF, because it decides world policy on climate

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The General Assembly, because all members sit there with equal votes and any matter within the Charter can be discussed. The General Assembly is the world forum: universal membership, equal votes and wide powers of discussion. The Security Council has only fifteen members, the ICJ decides legal disputes, and UNICEF works for children.

questions.stem_md: Critics say the Security Council has sometimes stood still during serious conflicts even when most of its members wanted action. Which feature best explains this?

options.text_md: The veto, by which one permanent member can block a substantive decision
The rule that the Council has fifteen members
The fact that the Council meets in New York
The two-year term of non-permanent members

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The veto, by which one permanent member can block a substantive decision. A single permanent member's negative vote defeats a substantive resolution, so action can be blocked even when a large majority favours it. The other features do not stop decisions.

**Diary of an imagined Class 10 student, Model United Nations, Pune**

Today I represented a small island state. In the big hall, where every country had one seat and one vote, my speech on rising seas was heard just as long as the speech of the largest country. In the afternoon fifteen of us met in the smaller room. Our resolution on a ceasefire won eleven votes, but it still failed, because one delegate whose country holds a permanent seat raised her card against it. Our teacher said that this was how the real thing works.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): The student felt heard in the big hall. Give two reasons why small states value the General Assembly.

Today we remember the day when the nations of the world, meeting in Paris three years after the great war ended, agreed on a common list of the rights and freedoms that belong to every human being. questions.stem_md: In which month of 1945 was the United Nations Charter signed?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** June. The Charter was signed in June 1945 (26 June) and came into force in October 1945.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the General Assembly, a very small member state has the same single vote as the largest.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Each member state has one vote in the General Assembly.

questions.stem_md: The Security Council has five permanent and ___ non-permanent members.
questions.solution_md: There are ten non-permanent members, elected for two years.

questions.stem_md: Who among the following can use the veto in the Security Council?

options.text_md: Every member of the Security Council
Every member of the General Assembly

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Only the five permanent members. Only the five permanent members hold the veto; non-permanent members do not.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The International Court of Justice has fifteen judges.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The Court has fifteen judges, elected for nine years.

questions.stem_md: Which agency in this list has its headquarters in Geneva?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The World Health Organisation. The World Health Organisation is based in Geneva. UNICEF is in New York, UNESCO in Paris and the ICJ at The Hague.

questions.stem_md: UNESCO has its headquarters in the city of ___.
questions.solution_md: UNESCO's headquarters are in Paris.

questions.stem_md: In which year did the General Assembly adopt the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 1948. It was adopted on 10 December 1948.
